utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Before us we have the Prosecutor v. Zejnil Delalic, case No. IT‑96‑21‑T.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is a hearing on the motion filed by the Defence on defects in the form of the indictment. We have received that motion as well as various attachments and we have received the response from the Prosecutor as well as various attachments. Is the Defence ready to proceed and may I have the appearances for counsel, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic. I am counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I am ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, and for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Teresa McHenry for the Prosecutor. Senior trial attorney, Mr. Eric Ostberg, is still out of town. Miss Elles Van Dusschoten, trial manager, is also here at counsel table.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am trying to pull up the transcript and I am having some difficulty. One minute ‑‑ yes. It appears now that the transcript is operative. As I indicated, this is a hearing on the motion filed by the Defence, Mr. Delalic challenging the form of the indictment. We have received that motion as well as the response of the Prosecutor. Is the Defence ready to proceed and may I have appearances once again for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Defence, Ekrem Galijatovic and Edina Residovic. We are counsel for Mr. Delalic and we are ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Ms Residovic, will you be arguing this motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. My colleague and myself will present the arguments concerning the proposal we made in the Bosnian language on 4th July and in the English language on 8th July this year. Taking the right pursuant to Rule 73 concerning the previous motions on the form of the indictment, the Defence made a written motion and gave a large number of documents confirming and supporting that motion and later on informed the Tribunal that it will be using other explanations and other supporting material which it got in the meantime. Rule 47(B) stipulates that the indictment against an accused person should contain, 1st, the name and the details of the accused; second, the basics of the merits and then, third, the basics of the crime with which a person is charged. The Defence in a written motion declared in its submission that the indictment against Mr. Delalic does not contain any of these necessary conditions that are in the Rules, except for the 1st and the last name of the accused, Mr. Delalic. For those reasons, the Defence stipulates that the indictment is vague, unclear, contradictory and ungrounded. It, therefore, proposes then and now to this Trial Chamber to reject the indictment in all its charges against Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Allow me, please, to tell you for which reasons the Defence would like that. First of all, the Defence does not see all the expressions of the background and the facts, but it alleges that the legal Bosnian forces carried out many aggression on the areas with a majority of Serbian population, and it does not in the introduction take into account the fact that it was the time after the aggression, which it is clear in the indictment, in the charges 2 and 9, it clearly stated that it was an international aggression. That is why the indictment and the facts are unclear because it suggests a different development of events than was really the case. As in our written submission, we explained in more detail what it was all about. We, in our submission, think that such an indictment cannot stand and the most important part of our motion concerns the lack of information about the accused. Except for the 1st and the last name of Mr. Delalic, all the other information is so much contradictory that the whole indictment is ungrounded. Instead of a short account of the facts about the accused and its functions, in this part the Prosecution suggest that he, as co‑ordinator and then as a Commander of the Tactical Group No. 1, was in charge of the camps. That fact in itself is not linked to the actual function, but to Mr. Delalic. So, it is unclear in this particular part. In our submission, such allegations cannot stand when its validity is questioned. For the reasons of caution, in our motion we also mentioned other defects of the indictment. According to the Rule 47(B) ‑‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, if I can interrupt you because I should understand exactly what you are saying. If one looks at paragraph numbered 3 in the background, you have your client and the positions he is alleged to have held during the relevant period. I do not follow at all why you say that there is imprecision.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the indictment count which refers to the particulars of the accused, it is said that, as a co‑ordinator and then as the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group, he was the person superior in the camp. In them two completely different functions are indicated. Neither of these functions, regardless of either of them is a superior position, cannot run in parallel, because if he is a co‑ordinator, then he is not the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group. If he is the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group, then he is not the co‑ordinator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is my difficulty. This is all a matter of evidence. I do not follow at all why you say that there is inconsistency between those two positions. That will emerge in evidence, will it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe, your Honour, that it is necessary, 1st, to establish the capacity and if it is not done, if there are no particulars, there are inaccuracies, I know what you are referring to, but one and the same particular is expressed in two different ways. Therefore, these particulars become quite vague because we do not know whether the function of a Commander, whether the function of the co‑ordinator, means the supreme authority. Therefore, the Prosecutor should indeed be clear because such a contradiction regarding the principal capacity without which the accused Delalic could not appear before any court, let alone this one. That is why in the view of the Defence the indictment is so unclear, so vague, that we believe it should be dismissed. If I may, I should also briefly like to refer to another of the objections. It relates to some of the facts that, as the Rule says, the crime with which the suspect is charged. The indictment has very many facts about the crime in Celebici. Those are the objective grounds for incrimination for any superior. But that is not an act, the offence, of the superior. The superior, maybe the fact that he was aware of such acts and failed to act, yet this is not mentioned at all. The fact of the omission is not mentioned at all. All the indictment says is that he could have been aware of something, and yet failed to act upon it. In other words, the crime of which our defendant is accused, that is a crime for which a responsible commander needs to be accountable, but to become accountable, to become responsible, he must be a superior, yet this is not established. Your Honours, we already discussed this at our previous status conferences. The indictment speaks about acts which are tantamount to the omission to act, and yet no facts support this claim. So these are some of the defects of the indictment. We included some other objections in our motion, but I do not wish to dwell on them. I should merely like to respond to the response submitted by the Prosecution in writing. The Prosecution responds to the suggestions and submissions and the evidence we filed that during the preliminary hearings one cannot question a fact, and that the indictment contains all as required by Article 47(B). It thus rejects our 1st argument saying that it is not contradictory to items 9 and 10, and claims that items 9 and 10 presume the presence of some international forces in our territory which was not our intent. The intent of our motion referred to the contradiction of a situation wherein a country under Chapter VII of the United Nations is entitled to defends itself and is merely liberating territories occupied by an aggressor, that is, defending territories not occupied by that aggressor. In the light of this contradiction which the Prosecution also indicates, I think that the view of the Prosecution, that is, a political motion, does not hold water. This is a factual situation and it is not immaterial whether in a war conflict one detains prisoners or whether one detains civilians. I could not agree more that these are two categories of protected persons under the Geneva Conventions. However, the Prosecution should be consistent in either of the cases. Therefore, if we are talking about the capture of individuals in a conflict which is indispensable in order to liberate the territory and the town where these incidents are taking place, then this is quite unquestionable. The Prosecution also quotes a number of earlier rulings of the Tribunal in other similar cases and quotes the cases of Tadic, Mucic and some other opinions held by the Court. I do appreciate the law of precedents. However, since I come from a school of law which abides by the legality, and also in the light of the principle adopted by this Tribunal on individual responsibility, I do not think that the precedent made in a different case which has nothing similar to the status of our defendant can be accepted as an argument; all the more so as these are decisions of the Court still pending their entry into force. The precedent can only be observed, adopted, if we are talking about fully valid decisions. We, therefore, think that we should really follow those rules of law, or that system of law, which will best protect the interests of the accused or, rather, my defendant in this particular case. Furthermore, the Prosecutor indicates that even if the Chamber agreed that one could deliberate about the case in a manner requested by the Defence, it will refute that because the indictment has been confirmed by the Judges of this Tribunal. The rules of procedure do not envisage a specific procedure in that particular case, nor do they say that a Judge on a Chamber must follow the decision taken by the confirming Judge. The question arises, where is there the Rule 73 and preliminary motions, unless the Trial Chamber can rule differently from the confirming Judge. I do see such a possibility in the law of the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina and other Republics of the former Yugoslavia where various preliminary motions, submissions or objections to the indictment do exist. This right, this law, permits the Chamber that the subject of the indictment is not a crime, that there are extenuating circumstances such as, for instance, that my client was not a superior person in command and there is also not enough evidence to support the indictment. All those reasons which we indicate in our motion in writing and allegations of the Prosecution amount to what I have just said. But now, your Honours, while appreciating the fact that my client without having his capacity established has spent five months in a detention, I should also like to comment on those proofs and evidence that we submitted along with our motion. When referring to the question raised by your Honour, we believe that the indictment, in contrast with the Rules, establishes the possible existence of crimes in the Celebici camp, tends to forget the fact that a person may be responsible only if he is there in a particular capacity. If this capacity is not quoted in the indictment, then such charges against him simply cannot stand. With regard to the introductory part of the indictment and the number of evidence (and there is quite a pile of evidence), we wish to indicate the environment within which the Prosecution claims that crimes took place at Celebici. There were armed persons, and we have evidence about persons questioned at the time from which it transpires, clearly, that there were prisoners who, which is true, come under the protection of the Geneva Conventions. Therefore, if anybody committed a crime against them, he should be charged with that. To support our evidence, we also enclose the report of the investigating Commission which, likewise, established beyond any doubt that those were armed individuals. If need be, we may also submit to the trial the video tapes of the then situation in Konjic and Jablanica which may show that our motion, that our submission, regarding the introduction to the indictment is fully justified and that this evidence runs contrary to items 9 and 10 of the indictment. My client is in a very difficult predicament. I believe you should heed to that. He has been accused of severe war crime. When we talk about a war crime, we mean people who commit mass killings and so on and so forth. The Tribunal accuses Delalic of being a superior, and relates the superior position to Delalic. Whatever he might be doing, he is always a person superior, a person with authority, in that camp, and thereby it vests him with a specific capacity. In spite of the documents which date back to the time of the incidents and regardless of numerous testimonies of evidence, the Prosecution still insists that this is a person who was in command, a person of authority, regardless of the actual function that he held. I go back to the form of the indictment and I claim that the Prosecution must indicate very precisely the capacity of the defendant and know what he should be held accountable for. It is unquestionable that Delalic did not commit these crimes personally, that he did not order any crimes, that he was not a guard or warden of the camp, that he never talked to or investigated anyone in the camp, that he did not detain any person in person or order that somebody be detained. Therefore, having failed to do all that but, as the Prosecution says, was aware, or could be aware, that such and such acts were happening in the camp of Celebici, this awareness is not indicated in the indictment and thereby the indictment does not contain the facts on the omission. The Prosecution also claims that a relevant number of testimonies of prisoners corroborate the claims of the Prosecution. I am not producing evidence here, but I also have to go to the substance of the indictment if I am to refute the claims there. There is no doubt that persons captured, 1st, in blocked villages and then as prisoners are not in a position to know what functions were exercised by the accused Delalic. All they can say is that they saw him once pass through the camp and having heard that he was a person of importance. If this were true, some mention that he was the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group (which we have never denied) and this function is something that most of the witnesses remember. However, they have not the least idea what this function means. In view of this, among these numerous testimonies and documents that we submitted to the Trial Chamber, once again we also attached the statements of these persons who at that time did not mention Delalic as an eminent personality, let alone a superior person of authority. I must also add that recently in Belgrade a book came out with 48 testimonies of persons who went through the Celebici camp. None of those individuals mentions Mr. Delalic in any way whatsoever, not even the reports of the Helsinki Watch or the OSCE ever mention Mr. Delalic. What then led the Prosecutor to allege after all those books and after all this evidence that Mr. Delalic was a person of authority, that he was something, after we have learned about the file of the indictment that he suddenly emerges as a personality who is talked about? We have here an eminent newspaper which comes in Belgrade and on March 10th, that is only about 10 days before the arrest of Mr. Delalic, it came out with its issue which quotes in detail and in extenso all the counts of the indictment ‑‑ not even then. Therefore, your Honours, 10 days prior to the arrest of Mr. Delalic, when this extensive article mentions all the persons who have been transferred to this Tribunal, apart from Mr. Delalic, and very many other individuals from the area of Konjic, even then Mr. Delalic is not mentioned. However, my colleague, the counsel for Mr. Landzo, indicated the prejudice which arises with the arrest of Delalic. We have a large number of annexes, 23 different papers from Belgrade which subsequently start writing about Delalic as a mega criminal. I do not wish to belittle, to underestimate, the Prosecution in its attempt to prove the crime. Unfortunately, I must say they did nothing to establish whether my client was a person to appear between this Trial Chamber, or is this also an error in persona? What the Prosecution offers additionally in its response are statements of witnesses, of two witnesses, which are used, to all intents and purposes, as the grounds for all the charges with which my client is accused. I have to say that many witnesses we have offered before to the Tribunal and to the Trial Chamber had the opportunity to read that. Even something that somebody could judge as some kind of a superiority concerning [redacted] we showed to the Prosecutor the original video of two journalists, [redacted] [redacted] and [redacted] who at that time established a fact that, in complete contradiction with what those witnesses had said, the declarations made by the reporters and also by [redacted] that we are now giving to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecutor, because the Prosecutor in its response says that they are considering our proposals in detail, all these things show that Delalic had no superiority, no capacity, no official capacity and no contacts with the prison, except that in that context we could see the evidence made by [redacted] that know the situation in the prison. They say that they never saw Zejnil Delalic in that prison, nor that they ever had sent any report to him or had received any kind of similar report for the prison. At that time, as a co‑ordinator, Delalic [redacted] as Witness A, [redacted] [redacted] already had some threats expressed by some person coming from Herzegovina, and that is why [redacted] decided to be a protected witness. The second person, [redacted], when Mr. Delalic was the Commander of the Tactical Group, mentioned all the evidence. [redacted] there was never any information that either Mr. Delalic sent to the prison or that went from the prison to Mr. Delalic. We gave the evidence to the Prosecutor showing that Mr. Delalic had some contacts with the prison, but the Prosecutor used them in his response. We know that Mr. Delalic was on the premises of the prison because half of it belonged to the Logistics. He had to go to the prison to see all the arms that were there, all the weapons, but he had no official capacity in the actual prison. But all the persons interviewed show that Mr. Delalic had no reasons, no contacts, with the prison, apart from one which we gave to the Prosecutor after the visit of the ICRC, under the special order of the Supreme Command he is ordered to take some measures. The Supreme Command decided that one of the Commander of the Tactical Group (which had completely other duties) takes all the steps necessary to carry out a certain number of provisions. But, in the whole form of the indictment, I have to go back to a concise account of the facts that it should contain, but the Prosecutor never mentions with one single sentence where the responsibility of Zejnil Delalic towards the prison should appear. I am not going to interpret all this evidence, but I am not stating it just for the Trial Chamber to have to interpret them now, but just for the Trial Chamber to know that such evidence exists. We provided such evidence, even exculpatory evidence. There is a possibility always that the indictment be dismissed. We did not manage to convince the Prosecutor that Mr. Delalic was not a superior, but that is why we decided to show that there is contradiction with the list of the official capacities and the functions of Mr. Delalic, and also it is never stated where, under what order Mr. Delalic was appointed a superior. These are the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms Residovic. The evidence you have submitted to the Prosecutor that you contend supports your position that there is contradiction, that is, that Mr. Delalic was not in a superior position and he did not have responsibility over the Celebici camp, have you provided that to the Trial Chamber? You have provided much material in support of your motion for provisional release and the Trial Chamber had indicated that we would consider that, if you wished to submit it as a part of your challenge to the form of the indictment. But the information, the material, you are referring to now, has that been submitted to the Trial Chamber as a part of your motion for provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The document of 24th and 28th August in the very title, it can be see that according to the order given by the Supreme Command and the order made on 19th August, where it is asked from the prison Commander to take certain measures, that is, what Zejnil Delalic did was according to the order of the Supreme Command, not in his capacity as the Commander of the Tactical Group. We submitted that evidence in Bosnian and the English language. If you allow me, your Honour ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have a number of statements that you have submitted. I do not want to cut you short, but you have been preceding now for a little over half an hour and I wish you would bring it to an end. If I can just focus you, as you have indicated. At some point what we are concerned with, in terms of your challenge to the form of the indictment, is whether or not the indictment contains a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged. That is what Article 18(iv) provides, that the Prosecutor shall prepare an indictment containing the concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged under the Statute. Rule 47(B) of the rules of the Tribunal provides that, "The indictment shall set forth the name and particulars of the suspect, and a concise statement of the facts of the case and of the crime with which the suspect is charged". In your motion you have about, I think, six points, your written motion, but it appears to me that your argument really boils down to three points: (1) that Mr. Delalic is not a superior, that factually he is not a superior, that you have evidence that he was not in a position of responsibility over the Celebici camp. That is point (1). Point (2) is that the Prosecutor in the indictment has made a misstatement of the facts. First, in paragraph 2 of the indictment, the Prosecutor states that the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces attacked and took control of villages containing predominantly Serbs. It is your position that, in fact, they were not the aggressors. You also say then that the next assertion of the Prosecutor in paragraph 2 in which they assert that a state of international armed conflict existed is contradictory because of the allegation that is made in the earlier part of paragraph 2. The second part of your position that there is a misstatement of facts in the indictment relates to the Prosecutor's allegation that Mr. Delalic is a superior, that is, that he co‑ordinated activities, etc. etc. ‑‑ it is contained in paragraph 3 ‑‑ and the last sentence, "His responsibilities included authority over the Celebici camp and its personnel". You say that is a misstatement, that in fact his responsibilities did not include authority over the Celebici camp and its personnel. The third group of your arguments, it appears to me (and this is the one that I believe most closely meets our enquiry here in the light of Article 18.4 and Rule 47(B)), is whether or not the indictment contains a concise statement of facts. What you say is that in paragraph 3 of the indictment, when Mr. Delalic is described, those are not sufficient facts, that that allegation regarding his activities and the statement that his responsibilities included authority over the Celebici camp and its personnel does not meet the requirement of Rule 47(B) or Article 18(iv). Then you say in paragraph 7, when the Prosecutor states that Mr. Delalic had superior authority and knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were mistreating detainees and failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators, that once again there are not sufficient facts. The Prosecutor in its response says, "Well, these are matter of evidence". It is not their responsibility to provide in an indictment all the evidence that they have regarding Mr. Delalic's authority; nor are they responsible to provide evidence regarding its assertion that he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were mistreating detainees; that instead all they need do is set forth a concise statement of the facts and that evidence will come forward later. As my fellow Judge pointed out, if you disagree with the facts, I can understand that you disagree with the facts, Mr. Delalic has entered a plea of not guilty, but that alone is not sufficient to challenge the indictment itself. The question that we are focusing on is whether there is a concise statement of facts, so whether or not the indictment meets Article 18(iv) and Rule 47(B). As I say, you have three arguments, as I see it, only one of which really focuses on, I think, what the Trial Chamber is concerned with because we have reviewed the papers and discussed generally our view. You have filed a motion for provisional release. We have not ruled on the motion for provisional release. Attached to your motion for provisional release is a lot of data, and we do have some questions which we would like to pose regarding that motion and the data as soon as we conclude the hearing on this motion. So, unless you have something to add, I think we understand your position. We have read carefully the motion. We have read the attachments and we have heard you. But, unless you are going to give more information that we do not already have, I do not think that you are adding anything more. I do not want to cut you off, but I think we understand fully your position. So can you wrap up in five minutes? I guess I am cutting you off. Would you wrap up your argument in five minutes, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thank you for understanding my position, but I think that five minutes to let me state my position is not ‑‑ it is nothing to do with this understanding because my client is here, he has spent five months in custody, and we think not only there is not a concise statement of facts there, but there is no statement of facts in the indictment. There is the assertion that he knew or could have known. This is not a statement of fact. What did he know? When did he know? That would be a statement of fact about a superior, somebody in a superior capacity. That is not in the indictment. The Prosecutor did not put that in. That is why I ask for your understanding when we are in the situation when the Prosecutor is not giving all the burden of proof which would normally lay within the responsibility of the Prosecutor. Please allow the Defence to give evidence because we think it is necessary to show in this way what are the most important things in the case we are discussing. As the Trial Chamber did not rule on previous matters, we thought it necessary to stand and explain our position so that you could also have all the necessary material on which you could rule when you are going to rule about the separate trial and so on. There is nothing saying about the crimes of Mr. Delalic. There is the legal examination of facts when all those facts, statement of facts, are missing. So please allow me to say something on the last response of the Prosecutor made upon your request, your Honours, where there are also as an addendum the two statements of witnesses, [redacted] [redacted] and [redacted]. I will not ask here why two members of the HVO sent there to protect all the inmates in the camp, all these inmates who did not see Mr. Delalic, the person responsible for their situation. But, as we have said on previous occasions, these persons had some official functions in Konjic and that is maybe, therefore, why the Prosecutor believes them. But, if carefully read, their statements show that there are things missing and it should be very carefully examined by the Trial Chamber. Mr. Jorda probably in very short time with an enormous amount of material could not have all the time to look at that, because he also did not have all this enormous mass of material that we are providing and which was not provided by the Prosecutor. Unfortunately, in these two years that have elapsed since the events, a lot of material had accumulated. I will ask you for some 10 more minutes and I will wrap up in 10 minutes, and my colleague would also like to say something. That is how we agreed to ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So from what [redacted] is saying, one can say that he says that Mr. Delalic has been the Camp Commander, which nobody else had confirmed. There are so many things that are stated that are wrong. For example, that the defendant had been tried and sentenced by a Bosnian court to a 12‑year prison sentence. My defendant had not ever been accused of any ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, to make what you are saying useful to me, at least, I should ask you why are you challenging this? Obviously, you will cross‑examine this witness when he comes along and says what he has said, that your client was a Commander. Well and good. If your cross‑examination is successful, we will disbelieve him. But it does no good at this stage saying, "Here is a witness who when he is called should not be believed", which is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry? Excuse me one minute. I think what Ms Residovic is doing is responding to the Prosecutor's response and, that is, you have attached witness statements, and now what Ms Residovic is doing is saying that that information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am happy to wait for my time to respond. The only thing that I wanted to ask is any names of witnesses or potential witnesses not be used in open court. We submitted them as confidential. I know the Defence attorney has used what she believes are names of potential witnesses. I would just ask that they be expunged from the record and not be used by anyone here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms Residovic, refer to the substance of the statement. If the Prosecutor has submitted it to us, we will be able to identify the statement. But quickly wrap up, please, your response and do not identify the names of the witnesses at this point, and the name will be expunged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, your Honours, for having used the names, but the response of the Prosecutor did not state that these names should not be mentioned. This is a public hearing. So, I would like also that there would be the same treatment of the witnesses for the Defence as the witnesses for the Prosecution. So, the witnesses themselves speak in such a way in order to cover their own responsibility. Those witnesses ‑‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not need to know the names of the witnesses at this point. That is not relevant at all to our consideration. What we are concerned with is that you wish to respond to what the Prosecutor has asserted. But once you need to finish now because I have told you in so many words what we are focusing on is whether there is a concise statement. That is what you need to be focusing on because you are not really assisting the Tribunal at all in this argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the only witnesses that partly give in their statements, the Prosecutor partly gives a small concise statement of facts. I have to say that these witnesses should be neither witnesses for the Prosecution nor for the Defence. Many other Prosecutors have stated that those people could be sitting here in the place of my client. Many of them are responsible for thefts and other criminal offences in Konjic. There is other material that we produced in order to support this, what we are saying, because those persons ‑‑ we have mentioned this a previous time and even today the Prosecutor in his response gives this material. That is why I have to analyse these things in this particular manner in front of this Trial Chamber. We are going to submit all the supporting materials, most of them in English, and when you will be ruling on this motion, please examine them very carefully in case we will not be able to discuss this in more detail today. That is why I ask you, please, to bear in mind all of these things.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms Residovic, those statements are not a part of the indictment. So, whether or not those statements are correct or not correct, or whether they truly give a concise statement, they are not in the indictment. The issue is once again whether the indictment contains a concise statement of facts. It is your position (and you have stated it very clearly) that it does not. You have told us why, that you say in paragraph 3 the Prosecutor says his responsibility included authority over the Celebici camp, and you want the Prosecutor to explain how and why, describe his responsibilities, explain what were his responsibilities that included control or direction of the Celebici camp. The same thing with paragraph 6. But those statements are not in the indictment. They are not in the indictment. So it really does not make any difference what those say, except what you are saying is that since they have more evidence it should be in the indictment, but that is a question of law. That is a question of law as to whether or not a Prosecutor in an indictment is responsible for putting in the indictment evidentiary matters and that is purely a question of law. I do not care how many statements they have, and you can tell me that their statements are wrong, you can tell me that they are right, but it does not make any difference. The question is, need those facts be in the indictment? You have argued that point well in your papers and you have argued it well again, that is, you say they should be in. We need to hear from the Prosecutor and then we will decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to wrap up in these 10 minutes where various persons have spoken, but I will not ask for more time. I just want to pay attention that the statement of facts corroborated with such statements, that this cannot be found in the indictment. These facts can be accessible to the Trial Chamber, so I ask the Trial Chamber to examine that carefully. In the material that we submit it states that my defendant was not the Commander in Celebici. He was not responsible for appointing the Commander of the camp or the Commander of the artillery, or he is not responsible, he is not bearing responsibility for anything stated in the indictment. There is also all the supporting material, all the documents issued by the institutions of a country that co‑operates with this Tribunal, because all this states is that Zejnil Delalic had nothing to do with the prison. So, please, pay attention to the documents that were issued by the state institution in 1996. There is the Territorial Defence Commander statement which states that himself with the HVO Commanders made all the appointments when the prison was set up. That Commander states that Zejnil Delalic proposed the Camp Commander, but that the actual appointment was made in the usual way, that is, the Commander of the HVO and the Commander of the Territorial Defence. Maybe in various other tribunals, in the tribunals that are not of such high rank as this one, this would be enough to say that this cannot result, such responsibility, such an appointment, could not result from such a capacity. If we examine carefully all the statements of witnesses (which after a rule I cannot mention), there are 30 of such statements, there are 100 documents speaking about the functions, the capacities and the competences of my defendant, you would see that there are contradictions and that there is not any ground to say that this indictment contains a concise statement of facts, and that would be all. I do not think I have spoken for more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry ‑‑ did you have something to add that has not been already argued?

utterances.speaker: MR. GALIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I find incomprehensible the existence of the Prosecution to keep this indictment and to oppose the requests of the Defence to review the indictment. Your Honours, I should like to ask you to merely read carefully paragraph 3 of the indictment on page 2 where it says that Zejnil Delalic co‑ordinated activities of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces in the Konjic area from approximately April '92 to September '92, and that he was the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group of the Bosnian Muslim forces from approximately June '92 to November '92. This is also already so contradictory that at one and the same time, from June to September, he is both treated as a co‑ordinator and a Commander of a tactical group. This ‑‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Why is that contradictory? These are merely titles. The roles may be completely coincident, one with the other. You are playing with words when you say it is contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GALIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may say they are contradictory because they are wrong because ‑‑ put your earphones on ‑‑ but does that mean that they are not a concise statement of facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GALIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It is precisely that, and I claim with full responsibility that no European Court would admit such an indictment, nor could it stand on its two feet legally in the light of modern provisions of criminal law. One needs to realise that a co‑ordinator is a completely different function which was performed by the accused Zejnil Delalic, and a Commander of a tactical group is a completely different function. While he was a co‑ordinator between Bosnian and Croatian armed forces, there was a separate Commander of the 1st Tactical Group, that is, until 27th July '92 the 1st Tactical Group was headed by another person and he was replaced by Zejnil Delalic after July 27th. Therefore, the question arises, if a Commander of the 1st Tactical Group is a superior, how could he then be also responsible as a co‑ordinator for these acts if after 27th July '92, when he was appointed the Commander of the 1st Tactical Group, then the question arises whether there was a co‑ordinator and whether that other co‑ordinator was responsible for the situation. In other words, the approach of the Prosecution is completely erroneous. I claim with full responsibility that the opinion presented by colleague, Ms Residovic, there is not a single statement of fact in the indictment as such which would show that even had Delalic been a superior, what would have been his submission regarding the supervision and any other activities had he been a superior. But you do not have a single fact in the whole description of his acts whether he had done something or had not done something even if he had been responsible. In what way had he acted or failed to act? I think that such an indictment cannot pass the most elementary test of accusation because, ladies and gentlemen, one of the fundamental human rights is the right to freedom, to quick and expeditious court proceedings, the protection of human rights and, of course, our profession has a role to play in it. You must realise that the examination of the indictment cannot come down to a merely formal procedure, that it must go to the substance of the matter, and that we, as the Defence of an independent country and a member of the United Nations, are showing that until 18th May '92 the accused Zejnil Delalic had no position whatsoever in the army or in the political or any other state agency, that he was merely responsible for logistics as evidenced by the documents of the official authorities of that time. That is not '96, but May '92. That is the period for which he is incriminated for and when he is accused of being a co‑ordinator. He became the co‑ordinator on 18th May '92 only. This is from the Chief of Staff of the army to show what a co‑ordinator is, that he is not a person superior to anyone else, that he has no authority to issue any orders, that he is merely a co‑ordinator. We also have a certificate of the 4th Corps that in the territory of Konjic, Zejnil Delalic was not appointed to the position of a Commander, nor did he have any other position of authority in the Territorial Defence. We also have such a certificate issued by the Municipality of Konjic. We also offer some diagrams showing that his title, the title of co‑ordinator, meant that he was responsible for information and mediation, that he was never in a command position or anything else. We also have a written proof that on 27th July '92 he was appointed a Commander of tactical group which was a purely military group and, as shown from the official diagram, it only included a few soldiers from some Territorial Defences. We also offer proof which the Prosecutor uses against Zejnil Delalic. It is his orders of 22nd and 24th August showing that he acted under orders of the Supreme Command, and that when he learned from the International Red Cross report and from the Chiefs of Staff of the Supreme Command that he merely carried out the order of the Supreme Command and that he did all that. We also submit yet another proof. That is the order of 28th August '92 signed by the President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and the then Commander, Alilovic, on 28th August, provisional command group JUG was formed at that time, and my client Zejnil Delalic is appointed Assistant Commander of that group responsible for logistics. Therefore, all the previous proof that he was always responsible for logistics is corroborated. As of 28th August '92, he joins the temporary command of the group JUG and where he is in the position of the Deputy Logistics Commander. I cannot understand, the Prosecution may be wrong and we have already had such a case in this Tribunal because a case was dismissed against one individual. In this case, the Prosecution denies objective proof so persistently, and wishes to prove at whatever cost the responsibility of Zejnil Delalic in spite of the existence of evidence to the contrary. I think you really have to appreciate this stand of the Defence. It is really not irrelevant whether this man will spend a year or two in prison. His health has collapsed. He has family problems, business problems and he will suffer defeat in all walks of life. It is up to us to every time act in the spirit of humanity and also in the spirit of the Charter of United Nations. After all, your Rules may also be reviewed by your superiors and there is absolutely no reason why he should not be released from detention. We have nothing against the proceedings being continued, but it is not inhumane to be relieved of the charges after two years only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was going to ask you, each of those documents that you refer to, sir, have been submitted to us as a part of your motion for provisional release. We are aware of them. We have read them carefully. You do not have to read them again. It is your position that those documents would mean that when the Prosecutor alleges in the indictment that his responsibilities included authority over the Celebici camp and its personnel, that the Prosecutor is wrong. That is what your position is and you would offer those documents for that position. This is a hearing on the motion challenging the form of the indictment. The issue is whether or not the indictment states concise facts, and that is what we are focusing on. We have those documents. They have been submitted in support of your motion for provisional release. We are going to consider those. So I hear you, but we have spent an hour and a half mostly arguing about whether or not Mr. Delalic is a superior. I can understand it, because I can tell from the way that you are presenting the evidence that you firmly believe that he was not. We will attempt to address those concerns. I just do not believe that they can be addressed as it relates to the motion challenging the form of the indictment. Now we will stand in recess for ‑‑ there are some questions that we wish to ask, Mr. Residovic, and then we will hear from Ms McHenry in response to this motion that we are here today to discuss. But, regarding your motion for provisional release, you did attach a statement from Bosnia‑Herzegovina, I do not recall the title of the officer, but in any case stating that Bosnia‑Herzegovina would comply with any order of this Tribunal directing Mr. Delalic to appear before the Tribunal for a trial or any hearings. The Trial Chamber is wondering whether, perhaps, it would not be helpful to us if we could hear in person from that individual. We have the letter and there is a seal at the bottom of it. His last name is Pasic, P‑A‑S‑I‑C.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When we take our recess, I want you to think about this and then respond when we return. The second question that we have is where the defendant is proposing that he would reside, if he were released. In the motion he states Bosnia‑Herzegovina. He also talks about Austria and Germany. So we want to know where it is that he would reside. Thirdly, I would like to know more information surrounding the arrest of Mr. Delalic, how he came to be arrested. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. When we return, we will hear from Ms McHenry on the motion that has been filed by the Defence challenging the form of the indictment saying that it does not contain a concise statement of facts. We will then hear from Ms Residovic regarding these questions and, perhaps, others that the Judges may have regarding your motion for provisional release. Then we will hear from Ms McHenry regarding that issue as well. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I talk to my client?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms Residovic, you may. (11.25 a.m.) (Short adjournment) (11.45 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, would you please respond? You probably will say, "Well, where do I begin?" Begin with the motion, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just briefly respond to the motion because most of our more detailed response about specific factual allegations, specific sentences, are in our written material, so unless you specifically ask me about something, I will just very briefly respond. With respect to the form of the indictment, the Prosecution believes that this indictment does provide notice of the nature of the crimes and a concise statement of the facts. As such, the Statute of this Tribunal and the Rules of this Tribunal have been more than satisfied. Indeed, this Chamber has already denied identical claims challenging the form of this exact indictment with respect to the co-accused Mucic. To the extent that the accused wishes additional particulars, those maybe found in not only the supporting material which the accused got immediately, but in the large amounts of additional material which we have given and continue to give to the Defence. I think that is really the issue here. I believe that the Defence concedes that there is a specific factual allegation in the indictment, which is that as co‑ordinator and as Commander he had responsibility over the camp, and they contend that this is wrong and, therefore, they wish to know the evidence upon which we base that factual assertion such that they can dispute it. We have in many, many different ways given them the material which gives the particulars upon which, the evidence upon which, we will rely in arguing that, as co‑ordinator and then as Commander, he had responsibility over the Celebici camp. The fundamental principle of both, I think, this Tribunal and other tribunals, including those in Europe, is, is what is going on fair to the Defence? Is the Defence able to prepare, to know what they are being charged with, the basis for it and prepare for trial? I do not think that there can be any argument among anyone involved with this case that the Defence is not able to prepare for trial. They have been amply able to get large amounts of material going to the exact nature of the roles of co‑ordinator and of Commander and of his exact authority over the Celebici camp. We continue to explore some of those issues with the Defence. We continue to provide each other with additional material. We are continuing our investigation in attempting to clarify some of the material given by the Defence. We will continue to do so, but to the extent that there is now (and we expect that there will continue to be) a disputed issue of fact, ultimately that will have to be resolved at trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, if I may, one minute. Your reference though to Mr. Mucic, Mr. Mucic is a co-accused, but Mr. Mucic filed a motion for particulars. In Mr. Mucic's motion for particulars, we treated it as a challenge to the sufficiency of the indictment. Then we assumed that he had already gone through the step of looking at the materials to determine whether or not he had sufficient particulars and then acted on his request for particulars. But Mr. Mucic, unlike Mr. Delalic, as I recall, and I do not have the motion before me ‑‑ I had it and I left it in my office ‑‑ Mr. Mucic did not challenge the sufficiency of the evidence to show that he was a superior, that is, a Commander, at Celebici. He certainly, as I recall, did not attempt to offer the volumes of evidence that the Defence has offered here to support a position that, in fact, he was not the Commander of the camp. To that extent, is there such an exact fit, as you might suggest?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It would be our position that there is an exact fit. Although your Honour is correct that there is a difference in that this accused has provided much material, the form of the indictment should not depend on whether or not the Defence is, in our view, inappropriately trying to argue the merits of the case. Mr. Mucic, in fact, denies that he was Commander of the camp for the majority of the time with which he is accused, but I believe that he is appropriately not attempting to resolve the merits with a motion on the form of the indictment or with a motion requesting particulars. So the fact that I believe that the accused here is inappropriately trying to argue the merits, I do not believe that should have any relevance. If anything, I believe this very detailed attempt to argue the merits supports our case, which is that all the material they need to know the facts, the evidence upon which we are relying, has been provided to them. That, I think, is the only enquiry for this court. Is the indictment sufficient under the Statute and under our Rules? I believe that it is the exact same position for Mr. Mucic and for Mr. Delalic, and we continue to maintain that this motion and this form of documents is not an appropriate way to resolve disputes of fact. Your Honour, that is basically with respect to our material, again other than to note that with respect to a protection for the Defence, our Rules provide that the protection is that a confirming Judge looks at the material and sees if there is prima facie evidence to submit, to support, a prima facie case. That has been done. There is no other avenue within our Rules with which a defendant can challenge the factual accuracy of the Prosecution's evidence prior to trial, nor should there be because, in fact, I think, as this case demonstrates, it is impossible to do so without the full opportunity for all the relevant facts, without the full opportunity for cross‑examination. If the Defence wants to suggest to the Tribunal that they change the Rules because they believe that the confirming Judge did not do it, I believe that is the appropriate enquiry. In fact, I think the Judges should not adopt such a different rule because it would create more problems, more delay and in the long run less protection. But, under our Rules the factual allegations must be tested ultimately at trial, although of course the Prosecution and Defence can do everything beforehand to try to resolve and narrow them, which we are attempting to do in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Yes, except that Ms Residovic has said that when the confirming Judge considered all the material he was not fully aware of the new material which she has submitted to you, and in your response of 14th August you indicated that you were also conducting an ongoing enquiry on the papers which have been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is right, and I agree that the confirming Judge did not have all the evidence. In fact, the confirming Judge did not have all our evidence. But the appropriate time for all the evidence to be considered is at trial. So, yes, I would agree with you that the confirming Judge did not say, "I have looked at all the evidence in this case both for and against and I have had an opportunity to test the bias of witnesses and explore some ambiguities etc., and I find that this is a good case" or even "that this case is beyond a reasonable doubt", but that is what the trial is for.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has filed a response to the Defence's motion for the provisional release. Since that time, perhaps you have received more data from counsel for Mr. Delalic, I am not sure, but from listening to Ms Residovic it seems there has been an ongoing exchange. In considering the motion for provisional release, if we may then set aside this motion for a moment, should not this Trial Chamber review the strength of the Prosecution's case as we find it at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I do not believe you should. (1) I do not believe there is any provision for it under the Rules, and (2) in cases like this I believe, as in fact Judge Jorda found ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In Djukic? Is that the one he found that health reasons would be the only reason for provisional release? Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that is what was found in the Djukic case, but I do not believe that is what I am referring to, but I cannot be sure, despite having had it in front of me a few seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Jorda's review of the indictment after he confirmed it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it would be in the decision in the Blaskic case rejecting a request for provisional release, in which the Judge found, "The Rules have incorporated the principle of preventive detention of accused persons because of the extreme gravity of the crimes for which they are being prosecuted by the International Tribunal, and for this reason subordinate any measure for provisional release to the existence of exceptional circumstances". They go on to say that in that case the exceptional circumstances would be the health of the accused. In this case where there are numerous particular problems that this Tribunal has that a national court does not have, certainly including the gravity of the offence, but also given that we do not have a national Police Force and we have much more limited ways to obtain the appearance of witnesses, there is a presumption of preventive detention and no provision for looking at the strengths of the Prosecution's case. I believe that you, in effect, would have very complicated mini trials in every single case which would ultimately delay and cause a larger number of problems, including for witnesses. So, no, I do not believe that there is any provision in these Rules for an examination of the strength of the case, nor do I believe that this Court should adopt such a rule.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rule 65(B) says: "Release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances, after hearing the host country and only if it is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person". There is nothing in that Sub-rule nor anywhere else in Rule 65 that deals with provisional release that, at least, on its face would prevent the Trial Chamber from assessing again the strength of the Prosecutor's case, except that you say that has been the position of the other Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: There is certainly nothing in this, your Honour, I concede, in which it says on its face in exceptional circumstances should not include a review of the strength of the case. But, I also believe that, given that every accused believes that he is not guilty, had it been the case that your Honours intended exceptional circumstances to include the strength of the case, that would have been specifically set out as one of the factors to be considered in evaluating exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But if international standards require that we review periodically the strength of the Prosecutor's case in passing on a motion for provisional release, even though it is not specifically set forth in our Rule, would we not have to comply with those international standards and read them into 65(B)? I suppose the answer has to be yes, how can you say no? You would say those are not the international standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, they are not and, if so, the Rules should be amended to have some very specific procedure set out to control what I believe turns out to be an uncontrollable situation, at least as it exists now, and to the extent that in our system there has already been a finding by a Judge that there is sufficient evidence to charge someone, that in fact the international standards have been complied with, although I will concede that I am not an expert and have not looked at the exact standards for that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is correct. Judge Jorda did, I presume, confirm this indictment ‑‑ yes, I guess you have the review. It was Judge Jorda. Certainly he was acting based upon the evidence that was offered to him, the material of the Prosecutor, and all of that material now has been provided to the Defence. My only question was, well, what do we do as time goes on and further evidence is adduced either on the part of the Defence or either on the part of the Prosecutor? Should we stand firm with a determination that was made, perhaps, six months ago ‑‑ I am not sure when the indictment was confirmed ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The other question is this, and that was raised by Ms Residovic also, that is, that is just another Trial Chamber. In terms of precedent, it was either Ms Residovic or co‑counsel ‑‑ I am not sure which ‑‑ that would be not be a binding present on this Trial Chamber. What is your position in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not sure what you mean by "binding precedent". It is not binding on you in the sense that at trial you will be making your own decision. In fact, as I understand the Rules, they have been set up such that you will hear the evidence at trial relatively fresh and not have reviewed the supporting material. To the extent that the Defence is now suggesting that you review the supporting material, you review all kinds of additional documents and, in effect, have a mini‑trial, because that is what we are talking about, evaluating the strength of the case, I do not think the prior decision would be binding on you. But, with respect to whether or not there is sufficient evidence to charge this defendant, I believe that has already been made, your Honours, and that is binding in that regard. Certainly your Honours will be making your own determination of whether or not the evidence in all its presentation is sufficient to find the accused guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that may be binding, his confirmation and his decision that at that moment, in March, there was sufficient material offered to establish a prima facie case. But since that time, if additional evidence has come into the possession of the Prosecutor, or is offered by the Defence, should we not look at that to determine whether or not provisional release would be appropriate under 65(B)?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My position, your Honour, is firmly that you should not, that especially, in effect, what you would be having would be a mini‑trial, and that, in fact, what we should do is wait for the trial. That is what the Rules envision. In fact, I think the fact that the Defence rejects some of the statements given to it by the Prosecution and says, "Well, yes, we concede that these statement say that, in fact, he was a co‑ordinator and he was a Commander and he did have responsibility over Celebici camp", but they say, "but those witnesses are biased", I do not believe there is any way, realistically, for your Honours to evaluate those statements without having the witnesses and, in effect, without having a trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have received what I suppose were sworn statements from various officials within the government of Bosnia‑Herzegovina setting out the dates on which Mr. Delalic was appointed to certain positions, saying that it was not until July 12th, if I recall, or sometime in July, that in fact he was appointed to ‑‑ was it co‑ordinator or is it Commander? I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The documents submitted by the Defence indicate that on 27th July the accused was given certain responsibilities over armed forces in an area. But the documents ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us suppose the confirming Judge confirms the indictment, and some months after that the Defence presents an affidavit saying that this Mr. Delalic who is named in the indictment is not the Mr. Delalic who was a Commander of the forces, and as such may or may not have had responsibility for Celebici camp, and that is the case that Ms Residovic is referring to that was handled by the other Trial Chamber where there was a case of mistaken identity and that person was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that person was released because the Prosecution dismissed ‑‑ I am not even sure if the accused ever came here. I do not, in fact, think the accused ever did arrive in The Hague, but I am not sure. But the evidence was presented to the Prosecution ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution, I believe, had done an investigation and determined that there was a problem. I am not familiar with the all the complexities of that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It does not make too much difference. I guess the principle, though, is that after the confirmation there may be facts that become available that should be taken into consideration. The question becomes: Should those facts only be weighed by the Prosecutor or should the Trial Chamber play a role in reviewing additional matters that come to it after the confirming Judge has made a decision? Is there room in the Rules for such a consideration? Your position is that it would be a mini‑trial, that Mr. Delalic has pleaded not guilty and he says that he did not have superior authority over the camp or did not have control over the camp, and that is something that should be resolved at trial. That is what trial is all about. When a person enters a plea of not guilty, they are saying, "No, I did not commit those offences", and he is denying each and every allegation in the indictment, including that he was the Commander and including that he had a responsibility over the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is exactly right. I believe the evidence may be presented to the Prosecution, but to the extent that there remains a contested issue of fact that matter must await trial. Let me just again, it is not the case that in this case the Defence even is saying the Prosecution has no evidence, or anything like that. They are just saying, "We do not agree with the evidence. In fact, the situation is much more complicated than the Prosecution would have you believe. Therefore, we are going to give you 100 documents and 30 witness statements and all these things and have you, in effect, find that there is not enough evidence". But I believe that it is conceded here that the Prosecution does have evidence; it is just that the Defence does not agree with the evidence put forward by the Prosecution. I believe that is a disputed issue of fact and it will fall on a number of things, including credibility of witnesses, and that can only be resolved at trial. That is the ultimate safeguard, but given that (1) the Judge has already confirmed it and (2) evidence can always be presented to the Prosecution who will look at it, it is its ethical duty, we believe, to look at it and investigate where appropriate, and the ultimate safeguard then is trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One question then of you and then we ask Ms Residovic to provide some responses to questions we had posed: What weight should be given to Bosnia‑Herzegovina's willingness to turn over Mr. Delalic? One of the statements that we have received in the voluminous material that has been submitted is from the Minister ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Minister for Justice.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: ‑‑‑ and he indicates that Bosnia‑Herzegovina guarantees the return of Mr. Delalic. What weight should be given to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: To the extent that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has turned over defendants, has turned over accused in the past, we certainly think that is a relevant consideration and applaud Bosnia for its co‑operation with the Tribunal. Given that, we do not believe that this guarantee is sufficient in any way and I will just briefly discuss that, other than to say that there is nothing exceptional about this case other than the fervency with which the accused argues, that any other accused could not come and claim exactly the same thing with respect to the specific guarantees. The guarantee is, in effect, a guarantee that if they have the defendant in their territory and are able to find him, and if their rules of law on extradition permits his extradition, then they will turn him over. This guarantee does not speak in any way to whether or not Bosnia will be able to, in effect, have custody of this defendant if he does not want them to have custody. In this regard, we will point out, among other things, that Bosnia itself had an arrest warrant for this accused in 1992 and was never able to execute it. At some later point, I believe, the charges were dropped but for some significant period of time they themselves had an outstanding arrest warrant. Again, we will point to the accused's significant financial resources and his ties to many different countries. I do not believe that there is anything in this guarantee or as a matter of fact that Bosnia would be able to guarantee that they would be able to have physical control over the accused at all times. Even if then they did arrest him, there would be at the minimum a several month delay while the legal proceedings were gone through, because when they arrest someone there is first a court review and then a subsequent appeal that, in fact, the other accused in this case exercised in challenging Bosnia's turning them over. They lost those challenges. I am not an expert in their extradition proceedings and do not know under what conditions they would in fact not be able to turn someone over. For instance, do they do their own independent review of the merits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Ms McHenry you refer to reference in the guarantee, so‑called, to the extradition laws of Bosnia. I do not see anything to that effect. It simply says: "The legal authorities of Bosnia, Bosnia‑Herzegovina undertake the obligation herewith to ensure that Delalic will be available to the ICT. Upon each request of the Tribunal the presence of Delalic will be ensured in The Hague or in any other place and in due time as it would be determined by the International Tribunal." What could be more clear and unqualified than that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I am referring to the last paragraph ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: ‑‑‑ which refers to, "This guarantee is issued in accordance with the obligations undertaken by the Republic", including their rules of law on extradition. At least to the extent with the other accused it is the case that before anyone was turned over Bosnia had to find that that the proceeding ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just read that. It says: "This guarantee is issued in accordance with the obligations undertaken by the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina towards the International Tribunal on the basis of the Rules of the Memorandum on agreement between the Government of the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina and the Prosecutor." That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Well, where is your difficulty there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because I believe that implicit in this guarantee is a ‑‑‑‑

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I want explicit, not implicit. There is nothing explicit at all about qualifications.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, let us assume there is. Let us assume that as it relates to two of the accused, they went through the proceedings they were entitled to under the law in Bosnia before extradition. Suppose Mr. Delalic was willing to waive that right and suppose he were to say, "I waive my right to insist upon exhaustion of the procedures that Bosnia‑Herzegovina has adopted as a precondition to extradition"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly if we had a binding decision from the appropriate authorities in Bosnia which may include the Bosnian Supreme Court or may include the Ministry of Justice, I have to say I do not know, I think that would satisfy at least that concern.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So the first question would be whether that is waivable, perhaps. In some systems there are certain rights I suppose that are not waivable, but my general understanding is that a challenge to extradition is something that may be waived. If that were to be done and if that were approved by a Bosnian court, then that impediment has gone. The other impediment is that they would have to locate him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Is there anything else you wish to add on that point, Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had indicated when we were hearing the motion on the form of the indictment that we would consider the motion for provisional release and the attachments and had the asked the Prosecutor to respond to those, but we have kind gone afield from the motion on the form of the indictment. So let me hear then Ms Residovic. There were questions we posed and perhaps some more we will want to ask you about this matter. First regarding the Minister, is it possible to have a representative of his appear before the Chamber to explain to the Chamber this undertaking that is made in the letter from Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my Defendant will personally assume the application to come. There are no difficulties concerning his appearance before the Court because at the time of the arrest in Germany, he himself without the presence of his attorney, he requested immediately to be extradited to the International Tribunal. As I have said, my defendant believes profoundly that he is innocent and therefore he has no reason not to appear. Another proof, his statement to the German Court that he does not request any procedures concerning the extradition, that he is ready to go immediately. The second thing is the document that you are referring to. It came from the Ministry of Justice following the consultation with the Supreme Court of Bosnia‑Herzegovina and the Ministry of the Interior Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina. In other words, all those authorities guarantee that they will comply with the orders of the Tribunal. In other words, we are not talking here about conventional extradition or the enforcement of the extradition law, but the commitment of the State to comply with the orders of the Tribunal as expediently as possible. I believe our country has been doing so from the beginning. Thirdly, I have asked my office in Sarajevo to establish contact with Minister Pasic immediately, and Minister Pasic in Sarajevo I believe should be able to confirm his attitude within an hour or so. I can now say that the Minister is quite ready to come and appear before the Court if invited to confirm it all. Of course, it would be in the interest of my defendant to be in Germany where he has his residence, but there is no problem if the Court rules so he will live in Konjic and respond to any summons of the Court because it is in his own interest. He is an innocent person. It would thus also save the costs. Even the request that we made today is related to the frequent mentions by the Prosecution of the enormous costs, travel and so on and so forth. I am quite ready to adduce all the evidence that my Defendant is indeed willing to help the Court to reach its decision as soon as possible. We simply need to bear this in mind. In view of the evidence that you will have available when deciding and that you will look into when ruling upon our motions, I think you should also bear in mind the costs of travel, of sojourn and everything else. Another thing, that is what kind of decisions this Chamber may be taken after Judge Jorda confirmed the indictment. There is a Rule in this Tribunal and it allows the Tribunal that if the Rules are inaccurate to then accept those Rules which are most suited to the supreme principles of international law and human rights, and the right to justice I believe is one of the fundamental rights. I have already referred to the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is quite true that it need not be applied, but to follow a precedent which has not yet entered into force in a case which is under way, cannot be applied in this case. If Mucic was ever the warden of a prison, he was no doubt a superior person, a person in authority, but in the case of Delalic we do not have that situation. So that if this precedent which has not entered into force could be enforced, and I do not think so, then it certainly would not be suited to this situation because if the accused Mucic has spent a day as a warden of the prison, he is then responsible for that one day and our Defendant has not been a superior for one day, for a single day. So, you are quite right, and you should like to thank you for the commentary, the Judges need to go into additional material. They are not going to evaluate the evidence, but they need to have them at their disposal when ruling on our motion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding Mr. Delalic's place, his desire, you said it would be in his interests to be in Germany but he would live in Konjic, are you asking that if the Chamber grants provisional release he be permitted to reside in Germany? Judge Stephen wants to amplify on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: On this question of where he might reside, there are difficulties, are there not, in living in Germany? For instance, if he is to report daily, weekly or at some other period to appropriate authorities, that could scarcely be done in Germany I would have thought. It is unlikely that the German Police would assume that responsibility. What about in The Hague or in Bosnia? In The Hague I suppose he could report here. In Bosnia he could no doubt report to the Bosnian authorities. Have you any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know whether you have received our additional motion.
