We made a submission in response to the answer of the Netherlands Government with a guarantee of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina that it would guarantee all the costs of Mr. Delalic's sojourn here. Mr. Delalic would undertake to report to any agency as may be indicated by this Tribunal, but if you believe that the guarantee of the government of the Republic of Bosnia‑Herzegovina is the best guarantee that Mr. Delalic will respond to the summons of the Court, then Mr. Delalic could live in Konjic. That does not provide him with an identical opportunity for engaging in his business and solving other questions and problems, but he is quite willing to go to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One problem I suppose of living here in The Hague is that I gather you have not yet heard from the Dutch authorities as to whether permission could be granted to him to reside temporarily here, is that right? I know that you made an application, but I assume you have not had a response yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have received an oral response, your Honour, and I am told that the Minister of Justice had established contact with the Tribunal. I do not know with whom. They said that their decision would depend on the ruling of this Court, and that they would maintain communication. Unfortunately, due to my absence from the Hague I did not have contact with Mr. Marro, so I do not know whether the communication has been established indeed or not. Another thing, in a written responses and today in the oral statement of the representative of the Prosecution it is said that my Defendant is a very well off man. We have presented to the Court the letters of his firm. Unfortunately, it is very bad and the situation of his family is also very bad, and to ensure the defence to which he is entitled to and that is one of his basic rights to have, to have a counsel of his choice, I believe his family has run into debt.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Am I correct that your order of preference for Mr. Delalic or Mr. Delalic's order of preference would be first to reside in Germany if he were released. The second preference would be Konjic and the third would be Germany ‑‑ you correct me if I am wrong ‑‑ I am sorry, the Netherlands, Germany, Konjic, Netherlands. Would that be his order of preference?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to say right away we cannot ensure the guarantees of the German authorities regarding those conditions, those terms that his Honour referred to. So even though that would be his wish, we do not think it realistic. We, therefore, suggest that the Court rules that he lives in Konjic because that is where he has his home. He can also communicate by telephone with his company and everything else. The third possibility is The Hague if the Dutch authorities allow him to stay here for the duration of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So the wish list, so to speak, would be Germany, Konjic and the Netherlands, but realistically it would be Konjic and then the Netherlands, The Hague? How could, though, Bosnia‑Herzegovina guard against Mr. Delalic's escape, going underground, so to speak? Even though the Dayton Accords have been signed, we have the Dayton Accords and the situation has improved, we still read in the newspaper that they certainly are not back to normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is only one danger and I do not think it will ever happen again, for the war across the territory happens again. During this trial and alongside the efforts of our country and the world over, I believe that for the duration of the trial or that it would happen ever again, and under these conditions our country is quite able of complying, of standing good on the guarantees that it has given and there are communications.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How would the Trial Chamber guard against interfering with witnesses? My fellow Judge is reminding me that that is one of our concerns. How would we guard against Mr. Delalic interfering with witnesses? You indicated in one response that the witnesses were of a different ethnicity and perhaps located in an area that he would not have access to. Is that correct, and is that still the situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the situation continues. He is accused of war crime against Serbs. How can he go to Serbia and contact those witnesses? On the other hand, he is charged by two Croats. How can he go there? How could he have any influence over them? Thirdly, he has no money. If it is true what the Prosecution say, that some of the witnesses are in the United States or Australia, my client cannot go there to influence them. Besides, those witnesses are not incriminating him and I do not see how he could influence those who were prisoners in the camp, so they would start incriminating him now. At the time I used I think ample evidence in favour of this. Besides he has already obtained so many of statements of witnesses and everything else while he was in detention, so there is no need for him to influence anyone and in his interests that he tells the truth for the time to which the indictment applies.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to concern for witnesses, there are witnesses in Bosnia and there are witnesses in the immediate Konjic area, and so we would echo those concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can you tell me this, Ms Residovic? What sort of limitations would you suggest as far as residence in Konjic is concerned, confined to his house there, to an area of one kilometre around the house and daily reporting? What comments do you have on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that you would hardly expect that he spent all the time in his house. So he would be able to move around Konjic, in Konjic or whatever is necessary for his business, that is to go to Sarajevo and to Konjic. That is about 50 kilometres distance and that is where he could report to the authorities informing them that he was going on a business trip to Sarajevo or elsewhere, but he would not leave the territory of Bosnia‑Herzegovina which is under the control of army of Bosnia‑Herzegovina. Of course, his travel documents could be seized and he could use those documents only when summoned by the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I was going to ask you about that. Surrender of passport would be an obvious step, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Surrender of identity document, however, would be impractical I imagine, would it, because he needs to show that from time to time in Konjic? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. With respect to his living in Konjic, in addition to there being witnesses there, again the Tribunal has publicly and stated many times its appreciation for Bosnia's co‑operation with the Tribunal. It is also the case that Konjic, though, is a local area that is, in effect, where the allegations in this case happened. That is where, for instance, the Defendant was previously able to get false identity documents. It is still the case that things are tense now. I believe I am correct in saying that there are still people out there who use false documents to travel from place to place. It is also the case with respect to reporting and local officials that, for instance, the other two accused I believe lived in their houses in the Konjic area for over two months or for approximately two months before they were arrested because of the local conditions there. So I am not as confident as your Honours may be that in fact we could assure protection of witnesses or any kind of reliable reporting or even the ultimate appearance of the accused. I believe that would need much more examination. With respect to having Mr. Pasic, the Justice Minister here, I am sure that would be a large inconvenience. I believe Bosnia does have a local representative, and at the minimum I would suggest that ‑‑ I do not of course think your Honours should even go this far, but if you want to go further, I would suggest at a minimum that the Court hear from her and everyone be allowed to explore some of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is the Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, she has appeared before the Tribunal on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honours, very briefly may I?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Madam Prosecutor says that my Defendant had forged documents. I already discussed it. It was a legally issued document to another name under wartime conditions when it was indispensable to ensure safe movement around and after two attempts had been made against him in that same area. Secondly, I think that this Court should rule on our motion and that is that the Prosecutor may not use evidence obtained from the accused. We have already submitted such a motion and the Prosecutor has been using and commenting on evidence obtained from the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms Residovic, does Mr. Delalic have anything to say with respect to his willingness to appear before the Tribunal for any hearings that we may set as well as trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, would you stand up, sir, a moment? THE ACCUSED DELALIC: Yes, with pleasure, because I have no reason not to appear at any time and I would really like for the proceedings in my case to start as soon as possible, because I believe that the Defence and I already have so much evidence and we shall prove that this is a libel, especially when it comes to two principal witnesses for the Prosecution. Besides, they are in the territory of Herceg‑Bosna they are not officially in our Federation. They are enemies of the territory where I come and where I should like to live. There are some details mentioned here and the guarantees and who should I report to. I think that is the concern of the guarantor. Our Minister of Justice issued this guarantee and it is this concerned how they will act towards me, what documents I will surrender to them or whatever. There is I think unnecessary concern. I do not think we need any stronger guarantee than that. The same one would apply for Germany without any problem or procedure. In Germany where I spent unnecessary 60 days, your Honours, unnecessary 60 days in solitary confinement, I could do nothing and I could not help either the Defence or the Prosecution regarding this misconception under which I was arrested. So, within three days, if need be, I can appear either for a short session or for the real trial. Besides, we have already agreed that we should complete the statements which the investigators wish to do during this week in its entirety, so as not to incur unnecessary costs regarding additional interviews and supplement to the statements already made. That is all that I would have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What we are concerned about of course is your not contacting any witnesses, persons who may have information regarding the charges that are against you. That is something that you would be absolutely prohibited from doing. If we enter an order directing that you not do that, then you may be subject to other charges, contempt of court, for example, and possibly other penalties if you contact witnesses. But most importantly that is something that you are not to do. You understand that? THE ACCUSED DELALIC: Yes, your Honour, I understand it clearly, but I do have to say a fact. If I wanted to do I can do it now and contact these witnesses. The fact that I am in prison now, that I am in custody, it does not mean anything because I have got counsel, I have got my family. I think there is too preoccupation about contacting the witnesses, but there are there are many people from the region who cannot appear in Konjic, [redacted] and [redacted], they shelled Konjic, they wanted to attempt to kill me. I also doubt that they will appear before this Court. They also know that these were false allegations. If they said this in newspapers, in the media before, they will not appear before this Court. So, your Honours, you should have no fear about me contacting the witnesses. I cannot go into the Republic of Croatia, neither to Herceg‑Bosna because they were in conflict with us and the fact that I was in the war on the Bosnian side and also knowing that I am here charged with crimes against Serbs, one cannot even imagine that I would go in the region where the witnesses are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among the materials that we offer there is also an appeal of all the witnesses for the Prosecution cannot even contact counsel for the Defence, let alone the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have anything else, Ms Residovic? Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Other than to once again say that there are witnesses in the immediate Konjic area. The Defence may not know the identity of all those witnesses, and certainly the accused's presence in the area would discourage witnesses from co‑operating with us. That in fact was one of the reasons that was cited by Judge Jorda in denying similar motions with respect to General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Delalic, thank you. In there is nothing else from counsel, we will rule shortly on the motion of the Defence with respect to the form of the indictment and also shortly on the Defence's motion for provisional release, as well as the motion on separate trials that is still pending. Yes, Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would ask for a brief delay in any decision on provisional release while we at least explore with the Bosnian authorities and some other potential issues that might arise were the accused to be released in the Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will have 10 days, is that enough time to submit a supplementary response?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you we will stand adjourned. (12.50 p.m.) (The court adjourned).
